title: Swe senior domain garbage collection
question: At a level useful for debugging production issues, how does garbage collection actually work, and how can it cause a service to have latency spikes?
idealAnswer:
Explains the basic mechanism at a useful level: the runtime periodically identifies objects no longer reachable from any live reference and reclaims their memory, rather than requiring manual free

Mentions generational collection as a common real-world optimization, most objects die young, so collectors scan a small young generation frequently and a larger old generation less often, and can explain why that's an efficiency win

Correctly connects GC to latency spikes: a 'stop-the-world' pause (especially a full/major collection) halts application threads while it runs, which shows up as a request latency spike or timeout right at that moment

Names a concrete cause of GC pressure that a senior engineer would actually go looking for, e.g. excessive short-lived object allocation in a hot path, or accidentally retaining objects (a growing cache, a listener list) that prevents them from being collected at all

Bonus: mentions a real mitigation, like tuning heap size or GC algorithm/settings, reducing allocation in hot paths, or picking a low-pause-time collector for latency-sensitive services
